headline: Bangladesh hikes fuel prices by Tk 20/litre, experts call for tax waivers
summary: The government increased prices of four major petroleum products by Tk 20 per litre, passing on higher import costs to consumers. Analysts are urging a waiver of import taxes instead of burdening citizens already facing inflation.
details: The Bangladesh government has increased the prices of all four major petroleum products by Tk 20 a litre. This move transfers a significant share of mounting higher import costs to consumers, who are already struggling with inflation.
Analysts are calling for the government to waive import taxes, which can be as high as 25% on diesel, rather than raising prices. They argue that this would alleviate the burden on the public.

Currently, the National Board of Revenue (NBR) collects 6% customs duty, 15% VAT, 2% advance tax, and 2% advance income tax on fuel imports. Since June 2025, the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation (BPC) has been calculating these duties based on invoice value.

This change means BPC is now paying approximately Tk 15-20 more per litre in duties and taxes across fuel products. In the first eight months of this year, the government collected Tk 10,555 crore in customs duties and taxes from diesel, crude oil, and petrol imports.

The price hike took effect after BPC warned the government that it might run out of funds to open letters of credit (LCs) for fuel imports by October without fresh financing. BPC reported losses of Tk 22,876 crore between March and August from settling LCs for imported fuel.

The corporation sought reimbursement as a government subsidy and urged a full waiver of import tariffs or duty assessment at a fixed rate until the US-Israel war on Iran ends. The tax burden on diesel imports alone rose from Tk 18.36 per litre in February to Tk 32.44 in August, peaking at Tk 38.90 in April.

M Shamsul Alam, energy adviser to the Consumers Association of Bangladesh, stated that the government should not treat fuel as a source of revenue during a crisis. He noted that BPC earned nearly Tk 50,000 crore in net profit over the past decade when import costs were lower.

Fuel is considered a strategic commodity, and its price impacts almost every sector of the economy. Rising fuel prices lead to increased costs for transport, production, and goods supply, inevitably creating fresh pressure on inflation for consumers.

Khondaker Golam Moazzem, research director at the Centre for Policy Dialogue, suggested that the pricing framework should allow the government to reduce taxes when international prices rise sharply. Such a provision could offer consumers some relief during periods of high global prices.

Selim Raihan, executive director of the South Asian Network on Economic Modelling, highlighted institutional weaknesses, limited transparency, and inefficiencies in procurement and distribution within Bangladesh's fuel sector. He argued that raising retail prices without addressing these structural issues risks shifting the burden of sectoral inefficiency onto consumers.

Raihan, also a professor at the University of Dhaka, advocates for a transparent fuel pricing rule that distinguishes between temporary global shocks and permanent domestic cost pressures. He recommends examining the tax structure on fuel, improving BPC governance, strengthening procurement efficiency, and reducing avoidable distribution costs.

headline_marked: [[13-year-old boy murdered in Cumilla]] over iPhone, Tk5,000 debt; linked to yaba gangs
headline: 13-year-old boy murdered in Cumilla over iPhone, Tk5,000 debt; linked to yaba gangs
summary: Thirteen-year-old Ishiat Shahriar Opratim was found dead outside Cumilla city after leaving home with his mother's iPhone. Police detained three young men aged 15-20, linking the murder to a Tk5,000 debt and the pervasive influence of yaba.
details: Thirteen-year-old Ishiat Shahriar Opratim was found dead in the hillocks outside Cumilla city on Saturday, a day after he left home with his mother’s iPhone. Police later found the phone at the home of one of three young men, aged 15 to 20, who have been detained in connection with his death.

The incident highlights a growing social crisis in Bangladesh, where the combination of young delinquents, quick money from selling phones, and disproportionate violence is increasingly linked to yaba abuse. A national survey estimates 8.2 million Bangladeshis use illegal drugs, with 2.3 million using yaba.

Last year, law enforcers seized a record 43.5 million yaba and similar pills. The drug, bought for Tk 80 in Myanmar, sells for Tk 150-200 in Bangladesh, with profits often flowing back through informal channels. This trade is reportedly linked to funding Myanmar's internal conflicts.

Chronic yaba users often suffer from paranoia, sleeplessness, and stimulant psychosis, leading to impulsive aggression. The daily cost of a yaba habit, often several hundred taka, can drive jobless individuals to commit crimes like snatching phones to fund their addiction.

Sociological theories suggest that when legitimate paths to success are blocked, some young men turn to illegitimate routes, often forming "kishor gangs." The Dhaka Metropolitan Police alone counts 118 such gangs in the capital, involved in selling, using, and fighting over yaba.

The issue also has a gendered dimension, with yaba feeding a performance of hyper-masculinity among jobless youth. Women are often recruited as couriers due to lower search likelihood, and also bear the brunt of domestic rage from addicted family members.

Despite the home minister's zero-tolerance policy, past "wars on drugs," like the 2018 crackdown that left hundreds dead, have failed to curb the trade, which soon boomed again. An overstretched and sometimes compromised police force struggles to enforce laws against deeply entrenched practices.

Effective zero-tolerance requires targeting the money and patrons, exemplified by the case of former MP Abdur Rahman Bodi, named as a yaba godfather but never charged. A narcotics financial intelligence cell to freeze assets of godfathers, not just carriers, is crucial.

Additionally, a unified border operation involving BGB, Coast Guard, and Navy with shared real-time intelligence is needed, alongside international support to curtail the supply chain. Choking the trade around Cox’s Bazar would also enhance Rohingya camp security.

Finally, educational institutions must be involved through screening programs and confidential referral lines in secondary schools to deter drug use and gang recruitment. The opposition also has a role to play in leading where the state cannot.
